text: Imagine a world where everything happens at once! You wake up, eat breakfast, go to school, play, and sleep all at the exact same moment. Chaos, right? How does the world stay organized and know when to do what?
Why do you think it gets dark at night and bright in the morning? What if the sun decided to stay up all the time? How would we know when it's time to sleep?

content.title: The Spinning Earth
content.description: Our Earth spins like a top while moving around the Sun. This gives us Day and Night! Imagine shining a flashlight on a spinning ball.

text: This amazing system is called Time. We measure time in seconds, minutes, and hours. A full cycle of day and night makes 24 hours, which is one Day. Let's learn some important words about Time!

content.hint: The time when the sun is up, or a full 24-hour period.

content.question: What causes day and night to happen?
options: The sun turns off like a giant light bulb.
The Earth spins around like a top.
The moon blocks the sun every day.

text: Think about your favorite festival or holiday. How do you know when it is coming? If someone says 'My birthday is next week!', how do they count the days? Explain this to your parents in your own words.

Ancient Indians used the position of the Sun and Moon to track time! They created the 'Panchang' (a Hindu calendar). Time is connected to the stars, space, and even math. Every time you look at a calendar, you are doing space math!

content.title: Make Your Own Week Wheel
content.description: Cut a circle from cardboard. Divide it into 7 slices like a pizza. Write the names of the 7 days (Monday to Sunday) in order. Pin an arrow in the center. Spin it to find out what day comes next!

content.title: Mixing up Today, Tomorrow, and Yesterday
content.description: Remember: Today is happening right now. Tomorrow is the future (like sleeping and waking up). Yesterday is in the past (it's already gone!).

content.tip: Ask students to list their daily routine and write 'Morning', 'Afternoon', or 'Night' next to each activity. This builds practical, intuitive understanding of time blocks.

text: Let's explore the months! Have you noticed how some months are very hot, some are rainy, and some are cold? Why do you think that happens?
Why do you think we need 12 different months? What would happen if we just had one long month with 365 days? How would we track the seasons?

content.title: Earth's Journey Around the Sun
content.description: As Earth travels around the Sun in a huge circle, the weather changes. A full trip takes one year, which we divide into 12 months!

text: A Year has 12 months. Some months have 30 days, some have 31. February is very special; it usually has 28 days! Long ago, the names for months came from ancient Roman gods or numbers (like 'Octo' for eight in October).

content.hint: A period of about 30 days. There are 12 of these in one year.

content.question: Which month is known for being special and having fewer days than all the rest?

text: Hold your hands in fists and look at your knuckles. The 'Knuckle Trick' helps you remember which months have 31 days (knuckles) and which have 30 (spaces). Try teaching this smart trick to your younger sibling or friend!
Months are not just numbers on paper. They tell farmers when to plant seeds and when to harvest. The cycle of months is deeply connected to nature, the weather, and the food we eat.

content.title: The Family Birthday Calendar
content.description: Write down the names of all 12 months on a big chart. Ask your friends and family for their birthdays, and write their names in the correct month box. Find out which month has the most celebrations!
